title: My Pi Agent Teams. Claude Code Leak SIGNAL. Harness Engineering
summary: Reacting to the Claude Code source leak, Dan argues the real signal is that the agent harness is the product: it owns deterministic code, token caching, orchestration, prompts, skills, and model control — Claude Code is worth ~2.5 billion ARR and models are being commoditized, so harness engineering is the highest-leverage skill. He demonstrates his own multi-team harness built on the Pi coding agent (pi.dev): a chat room where a single orchestrator agent receives all input and delegates to team leads (setup, UI generation teams A/B/C) and hyper-specialized workers (scaffold worker, view generator, animation specialist, soft and hard validators). The demo builds an Infinite UI system — a brand-consistent, multi-brand application for an agent security command center called Aegis — generating three new UI variants in parallel, mixing Claude Sonnet 4.6 with open-source MiniMax 2.7 and Step 3.5 Flash models per team. Mid-demo the open-source models stop responding, and the team leads break the no-writing rule to complete the work themselves, which Dan uses to showcase why multi-model, multi-team redundancy matters. He then tours the harness internals: the multi-team config file, .pi directory, per-agent front matter with hot-loaded skills and domain restrictions, expertise/mental-model files (~7K tokens) the agents maintain themselves, and reusable prompts (variables, instructions, workflow) where delegate is a literal tool and information-dense keywords drive the workflow. He explains his 80/20 split — Claude Code as a meta-builder for the system that builds the system — and pitches agentic security as a major business opportunity before the course pitch for Tactical Agentic Coding and Agentic Horizon.
what_you_learn: You learn the anatomy of an owned agent harness: why one orchestrator should be your only entry point, how to structure three-tier agent teams (orchestrator, leads, workers) with delegation-only leads and till-done task lists, and how per-agent system prompts, skills, expertise files, and domain locks turn a coding agent into a reusable team that solves problem classes instead of one-off tasks.

skills.name: Agent Harness Engineering
skills.description: Building and customizing your own agent harness on the Pi coding agent to own context, model, prompt, and tools instead of renting Claude Code's defaults.

skills.name: Multi-Agent Orchestration
skills.description: Running three-tier teams where an orchestrator delegates to leads and leads delegate to specialized workers, all coordinated through a single chat interface.

skills.name: Strategic Thinking
skills.description: Designing orchestrators and team leads as thinkers and delegators that never write files themselves, keeping hierarchy and execution cleanly separated.

skills.name: Task Management
skills.description: Replacing to-do lists with till-done lists where agents keep working until every task is complete rather than stopping at plan boundaries.

skills.name: Prompt Engineering
skills.description: Templated prompts with variables, instructions, and workflow sections that turn repeated work into one-shot commands against the team.

skills.name: Model Selection & Routing
skills.description: Running different models per team (Sonnet 4.6 alongside MiniMax 2.7 and Step 3.5 Flash) and swapping them via config for redundancy and cost control.

skills.name: Domain Modeling
skills.description: Restricting each agent to specific file paths and operations through front-matter domain config, critical for mid-to-large codebases.

learnings.title: The Claude Code leak signal: the agent harness is the product
learnings.detail: Dan's take on the leak is not features but leverage: the harness supplies deterministic code, token caching, agent orchestration, prompts, skills, and model control — without it there is no agentic coding at all. With Claude Code at ~2.5B ARR and models commoditizing, building a specialized harness for your own domain is one of the most viable skills an agentic engineer can learn.

learnings.title: Infinite UI system: solving problem classes, not one-off tasks
learnings.detail: The demo system generates unlimited UI variants inside a consistent brand. It is structured as brands (Aegis, AgentX, AgentDan) containing applications containing versioned branch trees, and the agent team operates this product end-to-end — Dan frames the shift as solving problem classes instead of prompting a single agent to build one UI.

learnings.title: Three-tier team architecture: orchestrator, leads, workers
learnings.detail: The full team has 15 unique agents; a reduced 9-agent min version runs in the demo. One orchestrator talks to multiple team leads (setup, UI generation A/B/C), and each lead manages hyper-specialized workers: scaffold worker, view generator, animation specialist, soft validators, hard validators, and a dropped brand analyst.

learnings.title: Single orchestrator entry point keeps input flat as teams scale
learnings.detail: Dan pastes one prompt into a chat room and only ever talks to the orchestrator. This is deliberate: your cognitive input must not scale with the number of agents, so all horizontal scaling happens behind the orchestrator while the human interface stays at one chat message.

learnings.title: Teach the orchestrator to prompt engineer
learnings.detail: The orchestrator rewrites Dan's rough input into a full detailed prompt before at-mentioning the setup team, and leads do the same for workers — a meta-meta pattern where the system carries the prompt-engineering skill so the human doesn't have to.

learnings.title: Till-done lists instead of to-do lists
learnings.detail: The system tracks a till-done list: agents work until every task is complete. Combined with delegation-only rules (orchestrators and leads think, plan, and delegate but never do raw file work), this keeps the hierarchy honest while guaranteeing completion.

learnings.title: Live failure case: open-source models stall and leads break the rules
learnings.detail: Teams A and B running MiniMax 2.7 and Step 3.5 Flash return no response mid-demo. The leads recognize the workers are down and write the components themselves, explicitly reasoning the task must complete — behavior Dan compares to a real lead engineer picking up the slack, and proof you need multiple models and teams so one failure does not sink the run.

learnings.title: Owning the harness means owning the file structure
learnings.detail: Inside the .pi directory Dan built a custom multi-team layout instead of the stock agents/commands/skills layout: a multi-team config YAML, an agents directory, and per-agent expertise files. Because he owns the harness he can define any file structure, config format, and team topology he wants — the core argument of the video.

learnings.title: Expertise files: agents maintain their own mental models
learnings.detail: Each agent has an expertise file (~7K tokens in the demo) where it tracks what it learns about its domain. Dan never edits these files; he only gave agents a ~75-line skill describing how to manage a mental model. When agents boot, they load their expertise — so every run compounds knowledge instead of starting from zero.

learnings.title: Front-matter specialization: skills, tools, and domain locks
learnings.detail: Agent definitions carry front matter with a hot-loaded expertise file, skills injected into the system prompt for stronger adherence, a tools list, and a domain block restricting where the agent can operate. Dan highlights domain specialization for mid-to-large codebases: agents scoped to just the frontend, backend, migrations, devops, or billing with focused context — one agent, one prompt, one purpose.

learnings.title: Reusable prompts and the delegate keyword
learnings.detail: A generate command takes parameters (brand, product, tree, count, prompt) in a variables-instructions-workflow format, and the orchestrator runs the workflow top to bottom. Delegate is literally a tool, and information-dense keywords like delegate to X team move maximum information through the chat — the pattern for building prompts against a team rather than a single agent.

learnings.title: Claude Code as meta-builder: the 80/20 split
learnings.detail: Dan still does ~80% of his work in Claude Code, but uses it to build the system that builds the system — treating Claude Code as a meta agent rather than the builder of the final product. Once the specialized Pi-based team exists, it outperforms any number of single Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI instances for that domain.

learnings.title: Agentic security is the business opportunity
learnings.detail: The demo product is an agent security command center where always-on agents watch logs for anomalies and threats in real time. Dan argues agentic security will be one of the biggest fields for years: anyone can already prompt an exploit, so companies will need agent-driven defense — a serious opportunity for engineers who can build agent teams.

learnings.title: Trust and scale is the 2026 theme
learnings.detail: The closing frame: the theme of 2026 is increasing trust in your agents to do larger scales of work over time. Harness engineering gives control of the core four, multi-agent orchestration gives scale, and the two together let teams of agents operate your product end to end — the channel's north star of agents that work while you sleep.

key_points: The Claude Code leak tells us the agent harness is the product.
Without the agent harness there are no agents, no agentic coding, no agentic engineering.
Your input to the system must not scale with the number of agents — always talk to one orchestrator.
Orchestrators and leads don't work; they think, plan, and delegate — workers build.
When the open-source model teams went silent, the leads broke the no-writing rule to finish the job — build redundancy into your teams.
Agent expertise files compound: every session your agents load and grow their mental models.
Delegate is a tool and a keyword — information-dense commands drive multi-agent workflows.
Use Claude Code as the meta-builder: 80% building the system that builds the system.
